title: The Spacecraft That Became a Lifeboat
summary: On 11 April 1970, three astronauts left Earth for the Moon.

chapters.title: The Spacecraft That Became a Lifeboat

paragraphs.text: On 11 April 1970, three astronauts left Earth for the Moon.
Jim Lovell, Fred Haise, and Jack Swigert were travelling aboard Apollo 13. Lovell and Haise were supposed to explore the lunar surface, while Swigert remained in orbit above them.
Their spacecraft had been divided into parts because each part had a different job.

The command module, Odyssey, carried the crew and would bring them through Earth's atmosphere at the end of the mission. Attached to it was a service module carrying systems such as fuel cells and oxygen tanks.
The lunar module, Aquarius, was designed to take two astronauts down to the Moon and lift them back into lunar orbit.
Together, the modules made a machine capable of a journey no single part could complete alone.
Two days after launch, the crew were far from Earth when an oxygen tank in the service module exploded.
Warning lights appeared. Readings changed. Lovell saw gas escaping into space.
The trouble was much worse than one faulty instrument.
The fuel cells used oxygen and hydrogen to produce electricity. They also produced water. Losing oxygen threatened the spacecraft's power supply as well as its life-support resources.
A mission intended to land on the Moon became a mission to get home.
There was no rescue spacecraft waiting nearby. Whatever the astronauts used would have to be something already aboard.
Mission Control in Houston worked with the crew to understand the damage. Controllers had to make decisions using information sent over radio from a spacecraft more than a day's travel from safety.
Odyssey needed to be shut down to preserve the power remaining in its batteries. Those batteries would be essential during the return through Earth's atmosphere.
The astronauts moved into Aquarius.
The lunar module had become a lifeboat.
But it had been designed for two people during a limited part of a normal mission. It now had to support three people for much longer while the damaged spacecraft travelled back to Earth.
Every available resource mattered.
Electricity had to be saved. Water had to be rationed, partly because it was needed to cool equipment. Systems that normally kept the cabin comfortable were turned off.
The spacecraft became cold. Moisture collected inside. Sleeping was difficult, and the men had little room to move.
Then another problem appeared in the air they were breathing.
People breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide. A spacecraft cannot simply open a window to let used air escape. It has to remove carbon dioxide from its closed cabin.
Apollo used containers of lithium hydroxide, a chemical that absorbed carbon dioxide. Aquarius carried containers for its planned two-person journey, but now three people were using up that capacity.
Odyssey carried additional containers.
Unfortunately, the command module's square containers did not fit the lunar module's round connections.
The crew had the needed chemical. The obstacle was getting air to flow through it.
Engineers on Earth assembled a solution using materials available aboard the spacecraft. These included plastic bags, cardboard, a spacesuit hose, and tape.
They built and checked the arrangement on the ground, then explained the steps to the astronauts by radio. The crew made an adapter that directed air through the command module's containers.
Carbon dioxide levels fell.
The improvised equipment was not a decorative addition or a clever experiment for later. It was part of keeping the cabin usable during the journey home.
The spacecraft also needed the right route.
It could not stop and reverse direction like a car on a road. Its speed and position had to be changed with carefully planned engine burns.
Apollo 13 passed around the Moon. The crew saw the world they would no longer land on, then began the long return toward Earth.
Aquarius's engine helped adjust the path. Each burn had to be calculated so that the spacecraft would reach Earth's atmosphere at a suitable angle.
Too shallow an approach could fail to bring it safely down. Too steep an approach would create dangerous heating and forces.
Controllers also had to plan how to restart Odyssey using the limited power still available. The command module's equipment had been cold and inactive for days.
On the final approach, the damaged service module was released. The astronauts could finally see the extent of the destruction outside their cabin. A large part of its outer structure was missing.
Then they left Aquarius and prepared Odyssey for re-entry.
Aquarius could keep them alive in space, but it did not have the command module's heat shield. It could not carry them safely through the atmosphere.
The lifeboat had to be abandoned before the last part of the rescue.
Odyssey separated from it and entered the air surrounding Earth.
For several minutes, the radio connection was lost as the hot gas around the capsule interfered with communication. Mission Control could not hurry the capsule or shorten that silence.
The signal returned.
Parachutes opened, and on 17 April the crew splashed down in the Pacific Ocean.
All three astronauts had survived.

The investigation traced the accident to damage and events involving the oxygen tank before the mission, including problems during ground testing. Equipment and procedures were changed for later flights.
Apollo 13 did not achieve its planned landing. It did reveal how much a space mission depended on people understanding the machinery well enough to use it in an emergency.
The small module built to land two people on the Moon had instead helped bring three people back to Earth.
Odyssey's heat shield completed a journey Aquarius could never finish.
Neither spacecraft alone was enough. Together with the work of the crew and the teams on the ground, their remaining systems provided a route home.
